sections.label: CLTPA used against two gangs
sections.summary: In 2017, CLTPA was used to cripple two gangs operating in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: In 2017, CLTPA was used to cripple two gangs operating in Singapore.

sections.label: CNB use of CLTPA
sections.summary: The Central Narcotics Bureau uses CLTPA, and many drug trafficking syndicates have been crippled using it.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) uses it, and many drug trafficking syndicates have been crippled using CLTPA.

sections.label: CLTPA use and detention orders
sections.summary: CLTPA use has helped keep the drug situation under control, but the criminal justice system must be used wherever possible; 192 Detention Orders were issued in 1998.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: So, the use of CLTPA has helped us keep the drug situation under control.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: But, and I have given instructions on this, the approach has to be that, wherever we can, we must use the criminal justice system and not CLTPA.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: In fact, if Members look at the Detention Orders (DOs) that are issued under CLTPA against drug traffickers, in 1998, there were 192 such DOs.

sections.label: Detention order numbers over time
sections.summary: In 2010 the number of Detention Orders was 317, and it is now just about 103.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In 2010, seven years ago, the number was 317.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Members will see from the chart, it is now just about 103.

sections.label: Drug seizures in Southeast Asia
sections.summary: Heroin and morphine seizures linked to opium production in Southeast Asia grew nearly 90% between 2010 and 2015, and 97% of the world's ketamine was seized in this region in 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The seizures of heroin and morphine related to the production of opium in Southeast Asia grew by nearly 90% in the five years between 2010 and 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The seizure of ketamine, if you look at what was seized in the world and what proportion was seized in this region, 97% of all ketamine seized in the world was from this region in 2015.

sections.label: Bill scope and Fourth Schedule
sections.summary: Clause 3 states the Bill applies to "activities of a criminal nature" to be specified in a new Fourth Schedule, giving the public clarity on activities that could be subject to a DO.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: That gives more clarity to the public and everyone on which types of activities could be the subject of a DO.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, clause 3 states that the Bill applies to "activities of a criminal nature" that will be specified in a new Fourth Schedule.

sections.label: Minister's decisions final
sections.summary: Clause 3 inserts a new section 30(2) stating that every decision of the Minister under section 30(1) is final.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Clause 3 of the Bill inserts a new section 30(2) which states that every decision of the Minister on a matter under section 30(1) is final.

sections.label: CLTPA judicial review grounds
sections.summary: Judicial review of the CLTPA remains available on the traditional grounds of illegality, irrationality and procedural irregularity.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: As I have said, that has always been the position under the CLTPA and accepted to be so by our Courts.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It will be available in respect of CLTPA on the traditional, well-established grounds – illegality, irrationality and procedural irregularity.

sections.label: Different conditions per supervisee
sections.summary: Clause 4 re-enacts sections 33(1) and (2), enabling the Minister to impose different prescribed conditions on each supervisee based on their risks and needs.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Section 33(1) and (2), which are repealed and re-enacted by clause 4, enables the Minister to impose different prescribed condition on each supervisee based on the different risks and needs of each supervisee.

sections.label: Renewal of the Act
sections.summary: The Bill seeks to renew the Act for a further five years with effect from 21 October 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Bill also seeks to renew the Act for a further five years with effect from 21 October 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It seeks to provide for extension for five years.

sections.label: Judges chair ACs
sections.summary: From March 2018, the ACs will be chaired by sitting Judges of the Supreme Court of Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: From March this year, 2018, the ACs will be chaired by sitting Judges of the Supreme Court of Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I have spoken with the Chief Justice on this and he is agreeable to have Judges chair the ACs.

sections.label: Detainees held for gang activity
sections.summary: In 2016, 91 of 109 detainees were detained because of secret society gang activity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In 2016, 91 of 109 detainees were detained because of secret society gang activity.

sections.label: CLTPA safeguards and appeal
sections.summary: A successful CLTPA detention appeal affects debate on clause 3 finality and birthed the new Fourth Schedule.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Of course, we need safeguards within CLTPA itself and, since the last time CLTPA was renewed, there has been a successful appeal on detention under CLTPA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: This case impacts our debate on the Bill for two reasons: (a) it sheds light on the implications of clause 3 that says the Minister's decision is final, and (b) its observations birthed the new Fourth Schedule specifying the serious criminal activities as legitimate grounds for a detention under the Bill.

sections.label: Clause 8 Fourth Schedule
sections.summary: Clause 8 puts in the new Fourth Schedule specifying the scope of criminal activities for detention and supervision orders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Clause 8 puts in the new Fourth Schedule which specifies the scope of criminal activities, the powers of detention and supervision orders may be exercised for.

sections.label: Fourth Schedule Organised Crimes Act
sections.summary: The Fourth Schedule refers to section 48(1) of the Organised Crimes Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: One thing worth noting about the Fourth Schedule is the reference to section 48(1) of the Organised Crimes Act.

sections.label: Clause 4 Police supervision restrictions
sections.summary: Clause 4 moves restrictions on those on Police supervision from the main Act to subsidiary legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Clause 4 purports to make the regime more flexible by moving the restrictions placed on those on Police supervision from the main Act to subsidiary legislation.

sections.label: Bill criminalises essential services strikes
sections.summary: The Bill criminalises strikes for essential services employees and provides a tool to maintain public safety and order.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Besides detention without trial and supervision orders, this Bill criminalises strikes for employees of essential services, something which drew public attention in 2012.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Although the repercussions of that strike then may not have been as deeply felt, a protracted strike on essential services can be quite severe.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: As this Bill continues to provide a necessary tool to maintain Singapore’s public safety, peace and good order, and the very fact that we need to deploy muscular laws to deter criminal syndicate activity on our shores and based on my own experience as a legal practitioner in the Government and in the private sector, I support this Bill.

sections.label: Fundamental amendments to temporary Act
sections.summary: The extension before the House includes fundamental amendments extending new powers under an ostensibly temporary Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Unlike many extensions the Government has sought for this Act since then, the one before the House today includes a few fundamental amendments, which are very significant and extend new powers to the Government for an Act which was ostensibly temporary.

sections.label: MHA statement on three detainees
sections.summary: MHA said evidence against three persons and their syndicate roles was reviewed after the Court of Appeal decision in Dan Tan's case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), in a statement on 18 January 2016, stated that "the evidence against the three persons and their roles in the syndicate were recently reviewed, after the Court of Appeal gave its decision in Dan Tan's case." It would appear that in light of the judgment in Tan Seet Eng, the Government became aware of the poor case against them in law, putting the three detainees on supervision orders instead.

sections.label: Clause 3 and judicial review
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Minister how new clause 3 will interact with future judicial review for CLTPA detainees given Tan Seet Eng.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: If so, what is the impulse behind this amendment Bill and is it justified?

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I seek the Minister’s clarification on how this new clause 3 will interact with the prospect of judicial review for individuals detained under CLTPA in future, in view of the Court of Appeal’s judgment in Tan Seet Eng.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: While clause 3 does not explicitly exclude the prospects of judicial review, unlike section 8(2)(b) of the ISA, it is a fact that more, not fewer, judicial review cases are coming up for adjudication in our Courts, challenging the lawfulness of Government decisions.

sections.label: Clause 3 limiting judicial review
sections.summary: The speaker says clause 3 appears to close the door and further limit the Judiciary's scope for judicial review in CLTPA cases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In and of itself, it would appear intuitively logical for judges to have maximum access to the Minister or the Executive's thought processes even if they cannot replace it with their own.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, clause 3 appears to be going against the grain, closing the door and further limiting the Judiciary’s scope for judicial review for CLTPA cases.

sections.label: Courts requiring Minister's information
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Minister to confirm whether Courts can require detailed background facts to decide on the lawfulness of a CLTPA detention.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: To this end, I would like to ask the Minister, in the event the Courts require the Minister to reveal detailed information on the background facts on any of the three instances to determine and assist the Court to decide on the lawfulness of a CLTPA detention for the purposes of judicial review, can the Minister confirm if the Courts will be able to do so?

sections.label: Clause 8 and overseas serious crime
sections.summary: The speaker asks what threshold of participation or facilitation in a serious crime overseas applies under section 48(1) of the OCA before CLTPA can be used.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The third point I wish to make extends to the inclusion of clause 8 which covers section 48(1) of the Organised Crime Act (OCA) in Schedule 4 of the Bill extends the reach of CLTPA, by way of legislation, to individuals who participate or facilitate a serious crime overseas.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: What is the threshold of participation or facilitation in a serious crime overseas as defined by section 48(1) of the OCA before the CLTPA can be employed against an individual?

sections.label: CLTPA as necessary final tool
sections.summary: The speaker says this House has affirmed CLTPA as a blunt but necessary tool of final resort, and notes detainee numbers fell from over 300 to 100.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Yet, time and again, this House has affirmed the CLTPA as a blunt but necessary tool, a tool of final resort, to battle against organised criminals in all their forms, a tool to protect law-abiding citizens who might be deterred from reporting or testifying about crimes due to the threat of reprisal.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I note from the statistics that the Minister has shown today that the number of suspects detained under the Act has fallen from more than 300 to just 100 in the past 10 years.

sections.label: Fourth Schedule and Minister's final decision
sections.summary: The Fourth Schedule lists criminal activities the CLTPA covers, while clause 3 makes the Minister's decisions on association, supervision and detention final.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Yes, the proposed Fourth Schedule helpfully lists, for the first time, the "activities of a criminal nature" the CLTPA covers.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But clause 3 makes "final" the Minister's decision as to whether a person has been associated with CLTPA criminal activities, whether it is necessary for a person to be subject to Police supervision and, importantly, whether it is necessary for a person to be detained.

sections.label: Judicial review at common law
sections.summary: Judicial review is confined at common law to illegality, procedural impropriety or irrationality, and the Minister said it will continue to be available.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is confined at common law to reviewing the illegality, procedural impropriety or irrationality of a decision-making process, Ministerial or otherwise.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is thus reassuring that, today, the Minister has said that this judicial review will continue to be available.

sections.label: Bill not overriding Dan Tan
sections.summary: The speaker is reassured that the amendment Bill's purpose is not to override the Dan Tan case and the apex Court's decision.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Again, I am reassured today, that this is not the case.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: That the purpose of this amendment Bill is not to parliamentarily override the case of Dan Tan and the apex Court's decision.

sections.label: Apex Court on scrutinising Minister's grounds
sections.summary: The apex Court said the Court is to closely scrutinise the Minister's grounds and consider objectively whether the decision is open to challenge.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The apex Court, or the Court of Appeal, said, in this case at paragraph 74, "The CLTPA vests a potentially draconian power in the Executive…Public safety, peace and good order can cover a wide spectrum of possible scenarios. … It is true that Parliament has vested this power in the Minister; but … the Court is to closely scrutinise the grounds put forward by the Minister and consider objectively whether, on the face of these grounds, the decision is open to challenge on the basis of illegality, irrationality or procedural impropriety".

sections.label: Apex Court rejected narrow role
sections.summary: The apex Court in Dan Tan rejected a narrow role and held the Court may and should examine whether the Minister's power is properly invoked.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The apex Court in Dan Tan flatly rejected such a narrow role and held that the Court may and, indeed, should examine whether the power vested in the Minister is being properly invoked.

sections.label: Written statement to judicial review Court
sections.summary: The speaker suggests the written statement under section 31 shown to the Advisory Committee also be made available to a judicial review Court.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In addition to having, as we do now, as I have learnt just today, that there will be a sitting judge who chairs this Advisory Committee, may I suggest humbly that the written statement of the GD or Police supervision that is made under the CLTPA's section 31 and that is shown to the Advisory Committee be also made available to a judicial review Court if the case so arises?

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I ask for this because I know that, even in the case of Dan Tan, this particular written notice was not made available to the Court of Appeal.

sections.label: Judicial review and clause 3
sections.summary: The speaker addresses Asst Prof Mohan's points on whether judicial review is available and whether clause 3 curtails it.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I thought if I dealt with one or two points in Asst Prof Mohan's speech, it might help the other Members in the House in their speeches so that we do not go off tangent.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think the crux of the Member's points is that: is judicial review available, and is clause 3 seeking to curtail that?

sections.label: Clause 3 and Dan Tan
sections.summary: Clause 3 sets out the current position from Dan Tan that the courts will not substitute their views for the Minister's on the facts.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Clause 3 simply sets out the current position which they themselves set out in Dan Tan that they will not substitute their views for the Minister's views on the facts.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: That is all that clause 3 does – crystalise the position as set out in Dan Tan.

sections.label: Dan Tan judicial review passages
sections.summary: The passages the Member read from the Dan Tan case on judicial review continue to apply.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It is there in the Dan Tan case.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And so, the passages that the Member read out from the Dan Tan case on judicial review continue to apply.

sections.label: Act extended to October 2019
sections.summary: At the 2013 renewal the Act was extended for five years from 21 October 2014, so it is due to lapse in October 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: At the last renewal in 2013, this Act was extended for five years from 21 October 2014, which means that it is only due to lapse in October 2019.

sections.label: Minister's detention power under section 30
sections.summary: Under existing section 30, the Minister can order detention not exceeding 12 months if satisfied it is necessary for public safety, peace and good order.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Under the existing section 30, the Minister can order detention of a person for any period not exceeding 12 months if the Minister is satisfied that it is necessary that the person be detained in the interest of public safety, peace and good order.

sections.label: Bill makes section 35 decisions final
sections.summary: The Bill proposes to make every decision of the Minister on the matter in the current section 35 final.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The Bill proposes to make every decision of the Minister on the matter in the current section 35 final.

sections.label: Detainees' judicial review rights
sections.summary: The proposed amendment removes detainees' existing rights to seek judicial review of the Minister's detention and supervision decisions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The proposed amendment is a disconcerting change to the existing provisions of the Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: I take the view that the proposed amendment will take away the existing rights of detainees under the current law to seek judicial review by our Courts in respect of the appropriateness of the Minister's decision to order any detention or supervision, specifically whether the Minister was correct in deciding that the person was appropriately associated with the type of criminal activities coming within the Act, or whether the Minister was correct in his decision that it was necessary for the person to be detained in the interest of public safety, peace and order, or whether the Minister was right in deciding that it was necessary to subject the person to the supervision of the Police.

sections.label: Court of Appeal Dan Tan judgment
sections.summary: The Court of Appeal's judgment confirmed the Court's role in checking the Minister's powers, and the amendment responds to Dan Tan's case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The Court of Appeal's decisive judgment confirmed the importance of the Court's role in ensuring that the Minister's order must fall within the scope of his powers under the current law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: There is no doubt that the proposed amendment is a response to the Court's decision in Dan Tan's case.

sections.label: Shifting review power to Courts
sections.summary: The speaker suggests the Minister still decide detention but review powers be given to the Courts instead of the President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: At present, the CLTPA is such that the Minister decides on the detention; the Advisory Committee advises the President and the President has ultimate powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: I would suggest that the Minister still decide on the detention but perhaps, powers of review be given to the Courts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: If Courts disagree and the judges disagree, then again, the Minister's decision will be overturned.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: So, remove it from the President to the Executive and give the power to the Courts.

sections.label: CLTPA history and opposition
sections.summary: The speaker is unable to support the Bill, noting the CLTPA was enacted in 1955 for an initial five-year period.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: This will also be in line with the extended period of detention accorded for a Police investigation under section 44(3) of the Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: And for that, I am unable to support this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The CLTPA was enacted in 1955 for an initial period of five years to make temporary provisions for the maintenance of public order.

sections.label: Successive five-year extensions
sections.summary: Parliament has extended the Act for successive five-year periods, with the current one due to expire on 20 October 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Because of this, Parliament has deemed it necessary to extend the Act for a further successive period of five years each time, which is now due to expire on 20 October 2019.

sections.label: Early extension timing query
sections.summary: The Bill extends the Act five years from 21 October 2019, which the speaker queries as about 20 months early.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding my position, I have a few queries for the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This Bill seeks to amend the Act to extend the operation of the Act for a further five years beginning on 21 October 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Given that this Act is only due to expire on 20 October 2019, it appears rather early to seek an extension of the Act approximately 20 months before it is due to expire.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This amounts to about one-third of the five-year extension period.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: It is apparent from the table that this is the earliest time before the expiry of the Act that an extension has been sought.

sections.label: Early extension reduces safeguard effect
sections.summary: Seeking extension before the Act expires reduces the safeguard because Parliament would lack current crime, security and drug information near expiry.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: Seeking an extension too early before expiry of the Act thus reduces the effect of the safeguard, as Parliament would not have the benefit of being apprised of the most current crime, security and drug situation in Singapore close to the expiry of the Act, to decide whether or not to extend it.

sections.label: Timing of extension and policy framework
sections.summary: A Member cites a 1981 amendment and asks why extension is sought now and what framework determines when approval is sought.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: For example, in 1981, before extension was sought in 1984, the Act was amended to enable detainees to be temporarily released from custody so that they could engage in outside employment to facilitate their rehabilitation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: I would be grateful if the hon Minister could please explain why the Government has decided to seek an extension of the Act at this point in time, which is quite some time far away from the expiry of the Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: Recognising that Parliament would need to be apprised of the latest security landscape in order to consider the case for extension of the Act, what is the Government's policy framework that determines when Parliamentary approval to extend the Act would be sought?

sections.label: Clause 3 and Minister's final position
sections.summary: Section 30, clause 3 is not intended to deal with judicial review but with the Minister's position being final.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Again, just to be clear, section 30, clause 3, is not intended to deal with judicial review.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It is to deal with the Minister's position being final, which is the position today – final in the sense that you cannot appeal on the facts for a different view of the facts to another body.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And if you look at the cases, that is the legal position.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It is not intended to touch on judicial review, on the classic principles that had been set out.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: As to why we have set out in the Schedule, it is precisely for the reason that the Member has said, to put some constraint and put it out clearly which legislation.

sections.label: Opposition to renewal timing and schedule
sections.summary: A Member says the Government has gone too far and focuses on renewal timing, the Fourth Schedule and clause 3.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: We did not delight in taking this position but did so with a heavy heart.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This time, however, our view is that the Government has gone too far.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: For my part, I will focus on three points: first, the timing of this renewal; secondly, the dangers of adding the Fourth Schedule to the Act; and thirdly, add my voice to the disapproval of clause 3 making the Minister's decision to detain final.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I agree totally with the hon Member Mr Murali Pillai and am surprised that Parliament is being asked to extend the Act now, in February 2018, when the current Act only expires in October 2019, 20 months from now, towards the end of next year.

sections.label: MHA renewal called premature
sections.summary: In the speaker's view, it is premature for MHA to ask Parliament now for a renewal of the Act.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In my view, it is premature of MHA to come to Parliament now to ask for a renewal of the Act.

sections.label: Bill increases Minister's powers
sections.summary: The Bill increases the Minister's powers.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Bill, in fact, increases the Minister’s powers.

sections.label: Court ruling on Dan Tan detention
sections.summary: The Court found the first detention order against Dan Tan did not further the CLTPA's purpose, declared it illegal and ordered his release.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Court had to look at the legal framework provided by the Act, what the Act is set out to achieve, the mischief it seeks to cure and whether the case made out by the Government on its face furthers that purpose.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: And because the Court was not satisfied that the first DO against Dan Tan furthered the purpose of CLTPA, the Court found that the Act could not apply to such a case and declared the first detention illegal, ordering him to be released.

sections.label: Fourth Schedule expands Minister's powers
sections.summary: The passage states that including the Fourth Schedule under clause 8 expands the Minister's powers over overseas criminal activities and the activities subject to the Act.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Contrary to what MHA has said, the inclusion of the Fourth Schedule under clause 8 clearly expands the Minister’s powers to police criminal activities overseas and expands the kinds of activities that are subject to the Act.

sections.label: Workers' Party opposes the Bill
sections.summary: The Workers' Party opposes the Bill, objecting to the finality clause and the Fourth Schedule, which it says expands the Minister's powers and the CLTPA's scope.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: More importantly, the Workers' Party does not see any justification to introduce a finality clause as proposed in clause 3.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In addition, I find the insertion of the Fourth Schedule under clause 8 to be dangerous, as it clearly expands the Minister’s powers rather than restricts them as claimed by MHA.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Bill will expand the scope of the CLTPA beyond its original intention of safeguarding peace and good order in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: These clauses will repose in the Minister of Home Affairs too much discretion and power, not only at home, but well beyond our shores.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: For these reasons, the Workers' Party opposes the Bill.

sections.label: Safeguards against CLTPA power abuse
sections.summary: The passage states CLTPA safeguards are not robust because checks are largely by the Executive, the Advisory Committee's recommendations are non-binding, and the President acts on Cabinet advice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: My position is that the safeguards to prevent an abuse of powers under the CLTPA is not sufficiently robust as the checks and balances are largely undertaken by the Executive, save for the consent of the Public Prosecutor and not by another independent arm of the Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Under section 30 of the CLTPA, while there is an Advisory Committee that will submit a report with recommendations on the Minister’s order to the President, the Advisory Committee's recommendation remains non-binding.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As such, even if the Advisory Committee recommends that the individual not be detained, the Minister is not legally obliged to follow the Advisory Committee’s recommendations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Further, while the President may confirm, vary or cancel the Minister’s orders, the President acts on the advice of the Cabinet which also comprises the Minister who made that order.

sections.label: Speaker unable to support amendments
sections.summary: The speaker states that during this debate he is not able to support the terms proposed in these amendments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: With this, Mr Speaker, and at this moment through this debate, I find myself not able to support the terms that are proposed in these amendments.

sections.label: Detention without trial and Article 9
sections.summary: The passage notes that the power to detain without trial under the Act is a significant exception to the Article 9 rule of law principle.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 2.10 pm until 2.30 pm.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: It bears reminding that the power to detain without trial under the Act is a significant exception to the fundamental rule of law principle enshrined under Article 9 of our Constitution that no person should be deprived of liberty without a fair trial.

sections.label: Advisory Committee recommendations not accepted
sections.summary: The Minister is asked for the number of cases in five years where Advisory Committee recommendations not to detain were not accepted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Minister provide information on the number of cases over the past five years in which the Advisory Committees make a recommendation not to detain but this recommendation was not accepted?

sections.label: Fourth Schedule offences under CLTPA
sections.summary: A question asks why the CLTPA needs to cover Fourth Schedule offences already dealt with under their own legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Another question raised is why there is a need for the CLTPA to cover the offences under the Fourth Schedule when these are already dealt with under their respective legislation?

sections.label: Support for Bill with restraint urged
sections.summary: A Member supports the Bill but urges the Government to use CLTPA powers with restraint and consider Advisory Committee recommendations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: In the spirit of "public safety, peace and good order", I stand in support of this Bill, but I urge the Government to exercise its powers under the CLTPA with great restraint, to provide full GDs, to take into account recommendations of the Advisory Committees, and to also provide reasons when recommendations are not accepted.

sections.label: CLTPA detainee numbers and Fourth Schedule
sections.summary: MHA is said to have been judicious, with detainee numbers falling to 109 in 2016, while the amendment Bill adds a Fourth Schedule.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, we note that MHA has been judicious in exercising the powers under the CLTPA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: There were 1,260 detainees in 1988 and it dropped more than half 10 years later in 1998 to 463, and, by 2008, the number has gone down to 290.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: In 2013, the figure dropped to 200 and it has been dropping yearly since then and reaching a record low of 109 in 2016.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: As observed in the annual report of the Singapore Prison Service (SPS) between 2013 and 2016, the types of criminal activities associated with CLTPA detainees were mainly drug trafficking, secret societies, unlicensed moneylending and a few others.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: However, the current CTPLA amendment Bill, amongst others, adopted a Fourth Schedule where a sizeable list of other crimes was also added.

sections.label: Detainees under 21 years old
sections.summary: The Singapore Prison Annual Report 2016 recorded two CLTPA detainees under 21 in 2016, five in 2015 and seven in 2014.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: According to the Singapore Prison Annual Report 2016, the number of detainees under CLTPA who were less than 21 years of age were two in 2016, five in 2015 and seven in 2014.

sections.label: Hearing outcomes and Advisory Committee names
sections.summary: A Member asks how long detainees and families wait to learn hearing outcomes and whether Advisory Committee members' names will be published.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: How long does it take for the detainee and family members to be informed of the outcome of the hearing?

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: I understand from the family member of the detainee that they may take up to six months before the hearing is made known to them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: In addition, will MHA consider publishing the names of the esteemed Advisory Committee members for better transparency?

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: The CLTPA is a tool which has clearly helped us to ensure the safety, peace and security of Singaporeans over the years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: This five-year Parliamentary review is a check and balance for us to periodically ask ourselves if the Act is still relevant, and I support the extension of the CLTPA for another five years.

sections.label: CLTPA detention of serious criminals
sections.summary: The CLTPA allows detention of persons in serious criminal activities when the normal criminal process is inadequate due to threats to witnesses or families.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: The CLTPA provides the avenue to allow for the detention of persons involved in serious criminal activities where the normal criminal process is found not to be adequate or sufficiently robust to deal with them because of the threat of harm to witnesses or their families.

sections.label: New Fourth Schedule criminal activities
sections.summary: The new Fourth Schedule will list criminal activities for which the Minister for Home Affairs can order detention or Police supervision under section 30.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: The new Fourth Schedule will list the types of criminal activities in relation to which the Minister for Home Affairs can make orders for detention or Police supervision under the above-mentioned section 30.

sections.label: Finality clause and fact-finding
sections.summary: The proposed finality clause reflects Parliament's intent to entrust fact-finding powers under the Act to the Minister and clarifies the Courts' position.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: The finality clause that is proposed in this Bill, therefore, reflects Parliament’s intent to entrust all relevant fact-finding powers under the Act to the Minister and clarifies the current position of the Courts.

sections.label: Singapore top Law and Order Index
sections.summary: In the Gallup Global Law and Order Report 2017, Singapore ranked top in the Law and Order Index, ahead of Iceland, Norway, Switzerland, Hong Kong and Japan.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: In the Gallup Global Law and Order Report 2017, Singapore was ranked top in the "Law and Order Index", ahead of other countries and cities like Iceland, Norway, Switzerland, Hong Kong and Japan.

sections.label: Clause 3 and successful appeal
sections.summary: The speaker says his view of clause 3 was clear and notes a successful appeal on CLTPA detention since the last renewal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: I think my view of clause 3 was clear in my speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: I said, since the last time the CLTPA was renewed, there has been a successful appeal on detention under the CLTPA.

sections.label: Clause 3 and Dan Tan judgment
sections.summary: The speaker maintains clause 3 does not change the law, citing the Tan Seet Eng judgment on judicial review of CLTPA detention.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Following Ms Sylvia Lim's clarification of me, I have studied the Dan Tan judgment and my position remains that just because clause 3 inserts subsection (2) to say that the Minister's decision is final, it does not change the law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: And the Court of Appeal in Tan Seet Eng, at paragraph 91 of the judgment, it was recognised, and I quote, "there is a fine line between assessment of the merits of the decision that is an evaluation of fact and policy and the assessment of whether the principles of just administrative action had been met." At paragraph 97 of the judgment, it goes on to say, "In our judgment, while it is one thing to say that the Court must not substitute its view as to the way in which the discretion that is vested in the Minister should be exercised, it is quite another to say the Minister's exercise of discretion may not be scrutinised by the Court at all." And here is the nub that the Court recognised, at paragraph 73 of the judgment, that "the correct scope of judicial review for this purpose in the context of the Order for Review of Detention (ORD) applications concerned with the detention under the CLTPA is a traditional test.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: What an applicant must show is that his detention is unlawful on the grounds of illegality, irrationality or procedural impropriety." Therefore, my conclusion, which is also evident in the first speech that I gave prior to the clarification, is that this inclusion of clause 3 only clarifies that the Court is not to substitute its own decision or look into the substantive merits of the decision.

sections.label: Residents' safety and security survey
sections.summary: 93% of residents feel safe walking in their neighbourhood at night and 92% rate Singapore's safety and security as good or very good.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Here, 93% of our residents say they feel safe when they walk in their neighbourhood at night; 92% say that they rate safety and security in Singapore as good or very good.

sections.label: UK knife and machete crime
sections.summary: The BBC reported a knife or blade was used in a UK crime every 16 minutes on average in 2016, with machete incidents rising over 60%.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: According to the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), a knife or blade was used in a crime every 16 minutes, on average, in the UK in 2016.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The number of incidents involving machetes has risen more than 60% in recent years.

sections.label: Gallup Poll police confidence
sections.summary: In the 2017 Gallup Poll, 57% of Americans had a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the Police, compared with Singapore's percentages in excess of 90%.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In the Gallup Poll in 2017, Americans with a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the Police stands at 57%, compared with our percentages in excess of 90%.

sections.label: Early intervention against gangs
sections.summary: Where gangs exist, they are intervened on very early and broken up, and are not allowed to reach this situation.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If there are gangs, and there are, we intervene very early and we break them up.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We do not allow them to get to this situation.

sections.label: Removing CLTPA and law order
sections.summary: Removing the CLTPA would not immediately lead to Sydney's situation, as Singapore has tough gun control laws, but a different law and order situation must be expected.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Supposing we remove the CLTPA, we are not immediately going to get to Sydney's situation straightaway; we have tough gun control laws as well, but you must expect a different law and order situation.

sections.label: CLTPA as police tool
sections.summary: The Police took a number of steps and did something about it, but the CLTPA is an essential tool in the arsenal for these things.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Police took a number of steps, did something about it, but the CLTPA is an essential tool in the arsenal of doing something about these things.

sections.label: CLTPA due process principle
sections.summary: The CLTPA rests on the principle that some criminals cannot be brought to justice through due process.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The principle behind CLTPA is that there will be some types of criminals where due process will not get them to justice, considering the nature of their duties.

sections.label: No exclusion of judicial review
sections.summary: Mr Pritam Singh said clause 3 narrows the judiciary's role, but the speaker repeated there is no exclusion of judicial review.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Pritam Singh said clause 3 operates to narrow the judiciary's role.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And I have said – I think by now I have said it about four, five times – there is no exclusion of judicial review.

sections.label: Courts not scrutinising detention evidence
sections.summary: The Courts are not to substitute their views of the facts or scrutinise the evidential basis for detention.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Courts are not to substitute their views of the facts or engage in an exercise of scrutinising the evidential basis for detention.

sections.label: Two requirements for detention
sections.summary: Detention now requires both section 30 requirements and Schedule listing, and listing alone does not permit automatic detention.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: All that is being done is that, on top of that, in addition to those grounds, the Minister has got to show that the offence or the nature of the activities are also listed in the Schedule.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Previously, there was one requirement, you show that the facts or requirements of section 30 are satisfied.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Now, there are two requirements, you got to show that the requirements of section 30 are satisfied and, in addition, that it has been listed in the Schedule.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It is not the case that if it is listed in the Schedule, the person can automatically be detained.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It has got to be shown that it was necessary to detain a person in the interests of public safety, peace and good order.

sections.label: CLTPA detention conditions
sections.summary: The CLTPA can detain a person associated with Fourth Schedule criminal activities if detention is necessary for public safety, peace and good order.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The CLTPA can be used to detain a person if he is associated with criminal activities, as stated in the Fourth Schedule, if detention is necessary in the interest of public safety, peace and good order in Singapore.

sections.label: CLTPA outside President's discretion
sections.summary: Matters relating to the CLTPA do not fall within the President's discretionary powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Matters relating to the CLTPA do not fall within the President's discretionary powers.

sections.label: Detention, Advisory Committee recommendations
sections.summary: About 17% of those detained were detained before, and Advisory Committees sometimes recommend against detention orders, which the Government usually accepts.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Of those currently under detention, about 17% have been placed under detention previously.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the number of cases over the last five years in which the Advisory Committees made a recommendation to detain but this was not accepted.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I can say this: Advisory Committees do, have done so, do recommend against DOs and, in the vast significant majority of these cases, the Government then accepts that advice and instead imposes PSOs.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But there have been a small number of cases where the Government disagrees.

sections.label: Orders referred to Advisory Committee
sections.summary: Under the CLTPA, all orders made by the Minister for Home Affairs must be referred to the Advisory Committee within 28 days of issuance.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In accordance with the CLTPA provisions, all orders made by the Minister for Home Affairs must be referred to the Advisory Committee within 28 days from its issuance.

sections.label: Advisory Committee report to President
sections.summary: The Advisory Committee submits a written report to the President, who can cancel, confirm or vary the order on Cabinet's advice.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Advisory Committee will consider and submit to the President a written report on the making of the orders and the recommendations.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The President will consider the report once it is received and can cancel, confirm or vary the order, but acting on the advice of Cabinet.

sections.label: Legal aid for detainees
sections.summary: The CLTPA is not covered by the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme, but detainees who cannot afford a lawyer can be referred to the Law Society.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: While the CLTPA is not covered by the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS), detainees who cannot afford a lawyer can be referred to the Law Society and they will assist.

sections.label: Voting on mistaken basis
sections.summary: Otherwise they will be voting on a mistaken basis as well.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Because, otherwise, they will be voting on a mistaken basis as well.

sections.label: Workers' Party renewal support conditions
sections.summary: Despite reservations about the renewal's timing being premature, the Workers' Party would have supported renewal if not for changes in clause 3 and clause 8.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: Despite my own reservations about the timing of the renewal being premature, the Workers' Party would have been prepared to support a renewal of the Act if not for these two changes in clause 3 and clause 8.

sections.label: Minister's decision final, non-appealability
sections.summary: The Minister's final decision concerns non-appealability and preventing courts or others from substituting their views.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: On the Minister's decision being final, that relates to non-appealability and not getting the Courts or anyone else to substitute their views for the Minister's views.

sections.label: Grounds of judicial review
sections.summary: Judicial review covers illegality, irrationality and procedural irregularity.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Judicial review is on illegality, irrationality, procedural irregularity.

sections.label: Reasons to amend detention law
sections.summary: The amendment is proposed because it is thought to improve the position of detainees, among others.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, to come back and say why do you want to amend, why not leave the current situation?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We think that this will improve the position, amongst others, of the detainees.

sections.label: Finality clause and Minister's facts
sections.summary: The finality clause makes clear the Minister's decision on the facts should not be appealed from.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The finality clause deals with something else, which is, the grounds on which the Minister makes the order, the facts and evidentiary bases which the Court of Appeal has said it would not scrutinise.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: What it does is, the legislation makes clear that the Minister's decision on the facts should not be appealed from.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, it makes it clear that you cannot go, for example, to the Courts and say, "I disagree with the Minister's decision on the facts for these reasons and I am effectively appealing and I am asking you to substitute your views for that of the Minister".

sections.label: Minister's decision and review processes
sections.summary: The Minister makes a decision, there is a series of processes, an Advisory Committee, and the Supreme Court has judicial review powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Minister makes a decision, there is a series of processes, Advisory Committee, the Supreme Court has the powers of judicial review over the Minister's decision.

sections.label: Court and Executive powers
sections.summary: Where the Executive acts within powers vested by Parliament, the Court is not concerned with whether it agrees with how those powers were exercised.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Paragraph 99: "Where the Executive is acting within the ambit of the powers that have been vested in it by Parliament, then the Court's concern is not with whether it agrees with the way in which the powers have been exercised.

sections.label: Advisory Committee judges from March
sections.summary: Three sitting Judges will chair the Advisory Committees from March, after agreement with the Chief Justice.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But UML is a good example – you use it effectively, you use other legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I told Members now we are picking up two persons under CLTPA per year, compared with 20 or so before 2011.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The current structure is also a tradeoff in that society then accepts that there are some risks in vesting this power in the Executive, which is what we try to reduce, restrain by the safeguards.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I have, for some time now, come to accept that the path we have taken is probably better for Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But at the same time, I did feel that the Advisory Committees could be strengthened and they could be strengthened in the way I suggested in 1994, not in 1989, but 1994.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: That is why I spoke with the Chief Justice, whether he would be happy to agree to have three of his sitting Judges sit on the Advisory Committee, chair the Advisory Committees, and he agreed.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We both felt it would be good for the process.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, from March this year, that will happen.

sections.label: Advisory Committee reports to President
sections.summary: The Advisory Committee reports to the President, who stands a little apart from the Executive branch.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Well, our sense is this: the Advisory Committee reports, in a way, to the President and you can say the Executive branch, but you know the President, of course, stands a little apart from the Executive branch.

sections.label: Judicial review material before Courts
sections.summary: Whatever is necessary for the judicial review is put before the Courts.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Whatever is necessary for the judicial review is put before the Courts.

sections.label: Rehabilitation directed for Prisons and DRC
sections.summary: The speaker directed Prisons and the CNB Drug Rehabilitation Centre to go much further on rehabilitation.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Some of these, for example, the changes to the supervising order, are really something that is quite close to my thinking.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I have directed Prisons and CNB Drug Rehabilitation Centre (DRC) to go much further on the rehabilitation line.

sections.label: Amendments bundled with five-year request
sections.summary: Other amendments were put together, and another five years was requested at the same time.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, we are making some other amendments and we put it all together.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And because we are coming to Parliament for the amendments, we said, "Okay, let us ask for another five years at the same time."

sections.label: Advisory Committee protects evidence and witnesses
sections.summary: Agreeing to the CLTPA required a process protecting information and witnesses, which is why the Advisory Committee exists.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: By 1994, I came to the conclusion that if you agree to the CLTPA, then you would have to agree to a process where the information and the witnesses are protected.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Which is why then you have this Advisory Committee.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They can receive evidence; they can choose to share some of it with the defence counsel; they may choose not to share some of it with the defence counsel; they have to look carefully to see what evidence they want; and they have got to be very careful that they do not expose some of the witnesses and their families to potential harm.

sections.label: Voting results declared
sections.summary: The voting results are declared as 77 Ayes, 10 Noes and two Abstentions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: I will proceed to declare the voting results now.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: There are 77 "Ayes", 10 "Noes", and two "Abstentions".

sections.label: Voting results declared
sections.summary: The voting results are declared as 77 Ayes, 10 Noes and two Abstentions.

sentences.speaker: The Chairman
sentences.text: I will proceed to declare the voting results now.

sentences.speaker: The Chairman
sentences.text: There are 77 "Ayes", 10 "Noes" and two "Abstentions".
